attrs.management_says: Receivables increased $118.4M (cited as a use of cash in working capital discussion). Receivables are recorded at shipment with credit terms to wholesale customers; retail/DTC collected in days.
attrs.numbers_show: Receivables grew 28.6% vs revenue 12.5%; DSO rose 39→45 days. Quarter signals: Q3 revenue +15.1% but receivables +31.4% (DSO 39→45); Q4 revenue +23.1%, receivables +28.6% (DSO 42→44). International wholesale (credit terms) grew 19.8% and distributor sales (credit terms) grew 24.6%, while DTC (cash) grew but is smaller. The mix shift toward higher-DSO international wholesale channels explains part of the receivables buildup, but management does not attribute the DSO rise to this mix shift or to any change in terms/timing.

attrs.reason: Management cites a $118.4M receivables increase and describes credit policy (E55) but does not attribute the 28.6% receivables growth vs 12.5% revenue growth (E25) or the 6-day DSO rise to any driver (e.g., channel mix shift). While segment data shows international wholesale/distributor growth (E44, E47), management does not make this causal link in its explanation.

rebuttal.innocent_explanation: The 6-day DSO increase (39 to 45 days) and 28.6% receivables growth versus 12.5% revenue growth are mechanically explained by the shift in revenue mix toward international wholesale and distributor channels, which inherently have longer collection periods due to credit terms. Segment data shows international wholesale sales grew 19.8% and distributor sales grew 24.6%, while domestic wholesale (shorter DSO) declined 1.0% and direct-to-consumer (cash-based) grew but remains smaller. Quarterly signals confirm DSO rose most in Q3 and Q4 when international wholesale growth was strongest. No change in credit terms or collection deterioration is required; the DSO rise is a composition effect.
